passage:
My roommate Bhavna has disliked her design diploma since the first term. She says so at night, quietly, with the lights off. But whenever I ask why she does not switch, she says, "I have already paid two years of fees and finished four semesters." She showed me the printed receipts in a folder tied with a rubber band, as if they were arguments. Last week she sat up until two rewriting a portfolio she called pointless. I cannot see inside her head, and maybe she is more hopeful than she lets on. But I noticed she talks about the fees more than the work. When a friend mentioned a coding bootcamp, Bhavna changed the subject and reached for the folder.
Tenzin

qa.q: What did Bhavna keep in a folder tied with a rubber band?
qa.a: Bhavna kept the printed receipts of her fees in the folder.

qa.q: What might Bhavna be feeling when she reaches for the folder?
qa.a: Anxious and stuck, unwilling to let go of the money and time already spent, though Tenzin cannot be certain.

qa.q: What question could help Bhavna decide about the diploma?
qa.a: Whether the coming semesters are worth it, because the fees already paid cannot be changed.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel when the idea of switching keeps being shut down?
qa.a: Frustrated and worried, but still willing to keep asking gently.

grounding: Illustrates a student who stays in a course that no longer fits because of what has already been paid and finished, seen by a roommate.

passage: On Saturday, Binita sat in a café while Tejas talked about the job he might take abroad without asking what she wanted, and she nodded, as she had for months. She thought, three years, I cannot waste them. On Wednesday she made a list for her sister of everything the two of them had done together, the trips and the birthdays, and could not write a single line about the coming year. On Sunday, on the bus, she asked herself a different question: if today were the first day, would I choose this? The answer came slowly, and it was no. It frightened her more than the list had. She decided to talk to Tejas after the weekend.

qa.q: What did Binita write for her sister on Wednesday?
qa.a: Binita made a list of everything she and Tejas had done together, the trips and the birthdays.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling on Saturday as she nodded at Tejas's plans?
qa.a: Small and unheard, yet reluctant to let three years go.

qa.q: What question helped Binita see things differently?
qa.a: She asked whether she would choose this relationship if today were the first day.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel when Binita talks to him?
qa.a: Probably surprised and hurt, since he may not have noticed how she felt while she kept nodding.

grounding: Illustrates a student who stays in a relationship because of years already invested even though it stopped fitting.

passage:
In Banda, everyone knew Rukmini was going to be a pharmacist. She was in the second year of her diploma at the town college. Her father had sold a buffalo to pay the first-year fees.
She was also, secretly, miserable. She fell asleep over drug tables. What she loved was teaching the neighbourhood children in the evening; she was good at it, and they came early.
One evening her cousin Kiran, home from Lucknow, found her crying over a chemistry book. "Why don't you do teacher training instead?"
"Two years, Kiran. The buffalo. Everyone knows. I can't throw that away."
Kiran sat down. "The buffalo is sold either way. The years are spent either way. What do the next forty years look like?"
Rukmini had never thought of it like that. She thought of forty years behind a counter.
The next week, she went with Kiran to the teacher training college to ask about admission, and she told her father she wanted to talk.

qa.q: What had Rukmini's father sold to pay the fees?
qa.a: Her father had sold a buffalo to pay the first-year fees.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel about the pharmacy course?
qa.a: Rukmini felt miserable and trapped, staying because of the money and years already spent.

qa.q: What question from Kiran changed how Rukmini saw the choice?
qa.a: "What do the next forty years look like?", which turned her attention from past effort to future value.

qa.q: How might Rukmini's father feel when she asks to talk?
qa.a: Her father might feel worried and disappointed at first, thinking of the buffalo, but could also be relieved to know what his daughter truly wants.

grounding: Shows a student who continues a course that no longer fits because of past investment, until a cousin helps her look at future value.

passage:
In Stockholm, Astrid and Ivan had been together since their first year of university, four years now. Lately they spent evenings in separate rooms. When Ivan talked about moving to his hometown after graduation, Astrid felt her stomach drop. She wanted to go abroad.
She told her friend Maja, "We just need to get through this phase."
"How long has the phase been?"
Astrid thought. "Since last spring."
"And why are you staying?"
"Four years, Maja. We've been through so much. His family is like mine. I can't just throw all that away."
"You're not throwing it away. It happened. It was good. The question is whether the next four years would be good."
Astrid didn't answer. That night, she sat with Ivan in the kitchen and said, "Can we talk honestly? Not about the past. About what we both want next." Ivan nodded slowly. It was the first real conversation in months.

qa.q: How long had Astrid and Ivan been together?
qa.a: Four years now, since their first year of university.

qa.q: How did Astrid feel when Ivan talked about moving to his hometown?
qa.a: Astrid felt a sinking dread, because she wanted to go abroad and their futures didn't match.

qa.q: What choice does Astrid make at the end, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She asks Ivan to talk honestly about what they both want next, shifting the decision from past investment to the future.

qa.q: How might Ivan feel when Astrid asks to talk?
qa.a: Ivan might feel nervous but also relieved, since it was their first real conversation in months.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who stays in a relationship that no longer fits because of years already invested, and begins to ask about the future instead.

passage:
In the career cell at his engineering college, Arnab sat across from Minakshi ma'am, the counsellor, with his marksheet folded into a small square.
"You've failed two mechanical papers this year," she said gently. "And last time you told me you spend every evening at the photography club."
"Yes, but I've done five semesters. Five. If I switch now, all of that goes to waste."
"What would the next three semesters look like if you stay?"
He unfolded the marksheet and folded it again. "More of this. Probably more backlogs."
"And the photography? The college magazine picked your pictures twice."
"That's just a hobby."
"Is it? Try this: forget the five semesters for a minute. If you were starting today, which would you choose?"
Arnab was quiet for a long time. The fan ticked overhead.
"Not mechanical," he finally said, and looked almost frightened by his own voice.

qa.q: How many semesters has Arnab done?
qa.a: Five semesters.

qa.q: What does Arnab folding and unfolding the marksheet suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Arnab feels anxious and torn, stuck between the five semesters already spent and a future he doesn't want.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi's question about starting today help?
qa.a: It set the past effort aside and made Arnab judge only what the coming years would bring, which is what should decide.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see Arnab calling photography "just a hobby"?
qa.a: Minakshi seems to doubt it, pointing out that the magazine picked the pictures twice and asking, "Is it?"

grounding: Shows a student staying on a course that no longer fits because of the semesters already invested.
